A 41-year-old female is evaluated in the emergency department after being involved in a motor vehicle
accident. During her workup, a non-contrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis reveals an incidental 2
cm mass in the pancreatic body, with no evidence of acute trauma. Her laboratory values, including
complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel, are within normal limits. She is discharged
with instructions to follow up with her primary care physician in one week. At the follow-up visit, she
reports no abdominal pain and her physical examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate
next diagnostic test to evaluate this pancreatic lesion? Answer Choices: (A) Fine needle aspiration
biopsy (B) Positron emission tomography (PET) scan (C) Magnetic resonance
cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) (D) Endoscopic ultrasound (E) Serum gastrin level (F) CEA (G)
Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (H) CA-125 (I) CA 19-9 level (J)
Serum chromogranin A level
 A. CEA
B. Endoscopic ultrasound
C. Serum chromogranin A level
D. Serum gastrin level
E. Positron emission tomography (PET) scan
F. Fine needle aspiration biopsy
G. CA-125
H. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast
I. CA 19-9 level
J. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)
